title: Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar on 26 August, 2013
full_text: Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar on 26 August, 2013 1 IN THE COURT OF SH SUNIL BENIWAL : METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE - 03 : SOUTH : SAKET COURT : NEW DELHI Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar CC No 123/1 U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act Unique Identification No. : 02406R0139192012 JUDGMENT (1) Serial number of the case : 123/1 (2) Name of the complainant : Afzal Ahmed S/o Abdul Gaffar Proprietor M/s A F Interior Contractor (3) Name of the accused, Mohinder Panwar parentage & residential address : s/o Late Sh Pyare Lal r/o B-1/15, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi (4) Offence complained of or proved : 138 Negotiable Instruments Act (5) Plea of the accused : Pleaded not guilty (6) Final Order : CONVICTED (7) Date of Institution : 07/03/2012 (8) Date on which reserved for judgment : 26/08/2013 (9) Date of Judgment : 26/08/2013 Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 1 of 21 2 BRIEF STATEMENT OF THE REASONS FOR THE DECISION The material facts as carved out from the complaint are that the complainant is a painter by profession and runs his business under the name & style of M/s A F Interior Contractor. Accused was known to the complainant and gave contract of painting, polishing at his above mentioned residential address and the complainant finished the said work as per the specification and satisfaction of the accused. Accused made payment from time to time to the complainant and lastly a sum of Rs.1,75,000/- was due upon the accused for the said job done by the complainant. The accused in discharge of his partial liability, issued a cheque of Rs.25,000/- bearing no. 000005 dated 22/10/2011 drawn on Kotak Mahindra Bank, Defence Colony, New Delhi in favour of A F Interior Contractor. The complainant presented the aforesaid cheque for encashment through his banker HDFC Bank. However, the same was returned dishonoured by the banker of accused State Bank of India, Siddharth Extension, New Delhi with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide memo dated 23/12/2011. Thereafter, the complainant made a demand for payment of the said amount of money by giving a Demand Notice dated 20/01/2012 to accused. Statutory notice of demand was duly served upon accused but he failed to make the payment of the said amount to complainant within stipulated time. Thereafter, the complainant has filed this complaint U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter "the Act") against the accused. Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 2 of 21 3 2. On 05.09.2012 after being satisfied that the complainant has a prima facie case against the accused, the court summoned accused for offence U/s 138 of the Act. 3. Accused appeared pursuant to the process issued by the court and on 05/07/2013, the particulars of the offence were read over and explained to the accused, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 4. In order to substantiate its case, the complainant examined himself and Sh Chet Ram as complainant witnesses. 5. All the circumstances appearing in the evidence against the accused were put to him in order to enable him to offer his explanation. In his statement U/s 313 CrPC recorded on 11/07/2013, accused stated that he had no liability to pay any amount to the complainant. Accused further stated that the complainant came to him on 21/10/2011 and after talking to him, he handed over the blank, self cheque to the complainant for purchasing material for painting. Accused further stated that in the evening, when he compared the rates with the other painters, he told accused not to start work. However, the said cheque remained with the complainant who did not return the same to him despite his demanding the same and later on the complainant misused the said cheque. Additional statement of accused was also recorded during the course of trial. Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 3 of 21 4 6. Accused examined himself in his defence evidence. 7. Arguments have been advanced by both the parties at length. It has been argued by Ld. counsel for the complainant that from evidence, he has proved that the cheque in question was signed by accused which was dishonoured and despite service of legal notice, accused did not make payment. It is argued that during cross examination of witnesses, no material contradictions have come out and the complainant has been able to prove his case to the hilt. It has been argued that accused has failed to rebutt the statutory presumption. Counsel for complainant has relied upon the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in C C Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed & anr . 8. Per contra, for knocking down the edifice of complainant case, it has been argued vehemently by Ld. counsel for defence that no case is made out against accused as he is innocent and complainant has misused the cheque in question. It has further been argued that accused has been able to successfully rebutt the presumption raised against him. Counsel for accused has relied upon the following judgments in support of his contentions : 1. HDFC Bank Ltd vs Amit Kumar Singh 2. Makaradhwaj Behera vs Satyanath Mahanta & anr. 2010 Cri.L.J. 983 Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 4 of 21 5 3. Patel Amrutbhai Narayandas vs State of Gujarat 2012 (2) DCR 74 9. I have heard both the parties at length and perused the record. Before entering into factual matrix of the present case, I deem it fit to discuss certain statutory provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act . Section 118 (A) of N I Act provides for presumptions regarding consideration for a Negotiable Instrument. It reads as under : "That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration". 10. Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides for presumption in favour of a holder. It reads as under : "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability". 11. Apex court in Rangappa vs Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 while overruling the judgment titled Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs Dattatraya G Hegde AIR 2008 SC 1325 observed in para 14 that : Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 5 of 21 6 "the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observation in Krishna Janardhan Bhatt (supra) cannot be correct............This is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested". 12. Therefore, in view of the statutory provisions and Apex Court's judgments, there is a presumption in favour of holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any legally enforceable debt or other liability. It is a well settled principle of law that the presumption available U/s 139 N I Act can be rebutted by the accused by adducing evidence. Therefore, the burden of proof is on the accused to rebutt this statutory presumption. The accused can prove the non existence of consideration by raising a probable defence and if he proves the same, then only the onus would shift upon complainant, who has to prove it as a matter of fact and his failure to prove would dis-entitle him to grant the relief. 13. Apex Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs Dattatraya G Hegde AIR 2008 Supreme Court 1325 has held as follows : "23. ...............Standard of proof on the part of an accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different". Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 6 of 21 7 14. I shall now appreciate the testimony of complainant to see whether the accused has discharged the burden of mandatory presumption or whether the guilt of accused has been proved beyond reasonable doubt by the complainant in the present case. The complainant who is the main witness in the present case was cross examined at length by the counsel for accused. In his cross examination, the witness has deposed as under : "I have not filed any document in this case showing myself as the proprietor of M/s A.F. Interior Contractors. There was no written agreement or contract between me and the accused for painting and polishing. The rates were also not settled in writing. I was referred to the accused by Taneja Paints, East of Kailash, near Sapna Cinema Hall, New Delhi. I have not filed any bill issued in the name of the accused in respect of the job done by me in this case. I worked for 2 - 2 ½ months in the said building. I have not mentioned names of any other painter employed by me for completing the job nor I have filed any attendance or other document to show such employment of labour by me. Yes, I had worked at the residence of the accused mentioned in the complaint i.e. B-1/15, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas, New Delhi. I have filled out the payee column on cheque ExCW1/A in my own handwriting. It is correct that legal notice ExCW1/C was sent at the address B-1/5, Shahpur Jat, Hauz Khas and not B-1/15. I cannot say whether there is any house situated at the address B-1/5, Shahpur Jat. As per my knowledge, accused told me that there is a house situated at the said address B-1/5, Shahpur Jat. I cannot say whether the address of accused is I (capital I) 5 and not B-1/5. It is correct that no acknowledgment of the notice ExCW1/C having been received by the accused has been filed on record by me. Accused may not have received the notice ExCW1/C. I do not know only God knows. It is wrong to suggest that I have never worked as a painter for the accused. Vol Accused has tendered cheques to me before the present case also. It is wrong to suggest that cheque Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 7 of 21 8 ExCW1/A was given to me as a self cheque in order for me to purchase the material. It is wrong to suggest that accused later on told me not to work for him after comparing rates with the other workers as I was charging more than the other workers. It is wrong to suggest that despite the accused's asking to return back the cheque ExCW1/A, I did not return the same and misused it after a period of about two months. It is wrong to suggest that accused did not have any legal liability to pay the cheque amount. It is incorrect to suggest that I have filed a false case against the accused." 15. CW-1 is complainant himself who has reiterated the averments of complaint in his affidavit of evidence. Complainant was cross examined at length by the Ld. counsel for accused. The whole testimony of the complainant seems to be reliable and trust worthy. Accused could not bring out anything in cross examination of complainant which may dent or demolish the case of the complainant. On the whole when the testimony of CW-1 is read along with the material available on record, it appears that the testimony of CW-1 is reliable and trustworthy and accused has failed to discharge the burden of mandatory presumption. In the statement of accused recorded as defence witness, accused had stated that he gave only one self cheque to the complainant but CW-2 Chet Ram, Manager from Delhi State Cooperative Bank was examined by the complainant who proved that accused had issued three more cheques in favour of the complainant in the sum of Rs.30,000/-, Rs.15,000/- and Rs.10,000/- respectively from the account of the accused. CW-2 proved the statement of account of the accused as ExCW2/3. Accused, right from the very beginning of the case, had tried to compromise the matter with the complainant. Counsel for Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 8 of 21 9 complainant has submitted that throughout the case, the accused had admitted his liability. Counsel for complainant has further submitted that no man of ordinary prudence would pay any sum of money to the other person if he does not have legal liability to pay to him and the accused from the very beginning of the case is ready to pay the cheque amount to the complainant. The story of the accused appears to be fishy and shows the conduct of the accused. The whole line of defence of the accused has been that mandatory legal notice under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act was not served upon the accused, therefore, the accused is not liable for commission of offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. Counsel for accused has also filed judgments supporting this aspect but none of these judgments are of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. But counsel for complainant has filed judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as C C Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed & anr ; more specifically para 17 of that judgment wherein the basis and principle of incorporating the service of mandatory legal notice for completion of offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act has been incorporated. When the judgment of C C Alavi Haji is read as a whole, it is clear that the intention of Hon'ble Supreme Court was to interpret this provision of mandatory legal notice in a harmonious way with all the objects and reason in enacting the statute of Negotiable Instruments Act . The very proviso of serving notice for dishonour of cheque upon the drawer of the cheque was incorporated so as to protect and save honest drawers of the cheque from futile prosecutions so that if the drawer had issued the cheque or Negotiable Instrument with a honest intention of paying the cheque Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 9 of 21 10 amount then he or she could come to know that the cheque issued by the drawer has gotten dishonored so that he could pay the cheque amount without throwing himself for the prosecution under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act for which the maximum sentence upon imprisonment could be two years imprisonment or fine upto twice the cheque amount (payable as compensation) or both. By no stretch of imagination could it be construed that the legislature intended that if the mandatory notice under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act was not served upon the drawer, then he could go scot free from his liability to pay the cheque amount. Accused cannot be granted this interpretation which defeats the very purpose of object of enacting the Negotiable Instruments Act and the stringent provisions therein for dishonour of a cheque issued by the drawer. 16. Banking system plays a vital role in business, trade, commercce and industry as well as in the development of a nation. When we talk about banking system, can the cheques which are very convenient and accepted mode of payment be ignored? The law regarding cheques, its ingredients, use, nature and criminal consequences of its bouncing is described in the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . Earlier dishonour of chceque was normally being covered within the purview of criminal offence of cheating under Section 420 of Indian Penal Code, however, it is very difficult to prove dishonest intention or knowledge, which can only be gathered by indirect ways as direct proof of the same is difficult to obtain. Most of the times, dishonour of cheque was treated as mere breach of promise and transaction Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 10 of 21 11 was treated as civil in nature generally resulting in acquittal from offence of cheating of issuer of cheque. Criminal prosecution also used to fail due to absence of 'mens-rea' or guilty mind and intention. Though an implied representation could be raised on the part of the issuer of the cheque that he would make all necessary arrangements for encashment of the cheque, still absence of basic ingredient of the offence of cheating i.e. Mens-rea, was difficult to be proved against opposite party. If the cheque accepted by a party in good faith is dishonoured with immunity and without any check, then it would lose its credibility, so to make the people realize their obligations while issuing cheques, the Parliament of India amended N I Act by adding Chapter XVII including Section 138 to 142 through "The Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instrument Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 (66 of 1988)" which came into force with effect from 1-4-89 by which the dishonor of cheque is made a criminal offence under Section 138 of N I Act. Certain more amendments were incorporated in these provisions and some more Sections were added in this chapter vide " The Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002 (Act no. 55 of 2002)". It came into force with effect from 6-2-2003. Since the provisions already in existence from Sections 138 to 142 in the N I Act were found deficient in dealing with dishonour of cheques, punishment provided was found to be inadequate, the procedure prescribed for the courts to deal with such matters was found to be cumbersome, courts were unable to decide the matters expeditiously, so these amendments in the Act were brought on record for disposal of cases, enhancing punishment for offenders, introducing Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 11 of 21 12 electronic image of a truncated cheque as well for exempting official nominee director from prosecution under the offence of Section 138 N I Act. 17. Supreme Court in case M/s Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd vs M/s Galaxy Traders & Agencies Ltd. 2001 (1) Crimes 198=2001 1 AD (SC) 409=(2001) 1 BC 684=AIR 2001 SC 676=2001 (1) RCR (Crl.) 646 held that the law relating to negotiable instruments is the law of commercial world, legislated to facilitate the activities in the trade and commerce, making provision of giving sanctity to the instrument of credit which would be deemed to be convertible into money and easily passable from one person to another. To achieve the objectives of the Act, the Legislature in its wisdom has thought it proper to make such provisions in the Act for conferring such privileges to the mercantile instruments contemplated under it and provide special penalties and procedure in case, the obligations under the instruments are not discharged. 18. Section 138 of N I Act specifically aims at persons who knowingly that they do not have sufficient funds in their bank accounts, issue cheques in favour of their creditors to discharge their liabilities. Thus the element of dishonesty is also involved in some situations on the part of those who issues cheques in such circumstances as the debtor put his creditor in awkward situation by issuing a cheque which he knows will not be honoured on presentation. Infact, Section 138 of the Act seeks to curb such dishonest acts. An honest debtor is not affected in view of the requirement of prior Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 12 of 21 13 mandatory notice to be given by the creditor to his debtor intimating about dishonour of cheque and time being allowed to the debtor to pay the cheque amount after service of notice as held by Delhi High Court in case Canbank Financial Services Ltd. Vs Gitanjali Motors Ltd 1995 Cri.L.J. 1222-1995 (1) Crimes 342=1995 (2) RCR (Crl.) 144 (Delhi). 19. The Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act 1988, inserted a new chapter XVII in the N I Act with following objected and reasons :- "to enhance the acceptability of cheques in settlement of liabilities by making the drawer liable for penalties in case of bouncing of cheques due to insufficiency of funds in the accounts or for the reason that it exceeds funds the arrangements made by the drawer, with adequate safeguards to prevent harassment of honest drawers". 20. The introduction of Section 138 in N I Act has made the dishonour of cheque penal so that a mischief that affects financial transactions, trade, business and ultimately the economy of country could be prevented or atleast curtailed. The Supreme Court of India has discussed usefulness of Section 138 in N I Act in case Shri Ishar Alloy Steels Ltd vs Jayaswals NECO Ltd 2001 11 AD (SC) 330=AIR 2001 SC 1161=2001 Cri.L.J. 1250=JT 2001 (3) SC 114=2001 (1) RCR (Crl.) 834=2001 (1) Crimes 284 in the following words : Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 13 of 21 14 "The law relating to Negotiable Instruments is the law of the commercial world which was enacted to facilitate the activities in trade and commerce making provision of giving sanctity to the instruments of credit which could be deemed to be convertible into money and easily passable from one person to another. In the absence of such instruments, the trade and commerce activities were likely to be adversely affected as it was not practicable for the trading community to carry on with it the bulk of the currency in force. The introduction of negotiable instruments owes its origin to the bartering system prevalent in the primitive society. The negotiable instruments are, infact, the instruments of credit being convertible on account of the legality of being negotiated and thus easily passable from one hand to another. The source of Indian law relating to such instruments is admittedly the English Common Law. The main object of the Act is to legalize the system by which instruments contemplated by it could pass from hand to hand by negotiation like any other goods. The purpose of the Act was to present an orderly and authoritative statement of the leading rules of law relating to the negotiable instruments. The Act intends mercantile instruments could be equated with ordinary goods passing from hand to hand. To achieve the objective of the Act, the Legislature in its wisdom thought it proper to make provision in the Act for conferring such privileges to the mercantile instruments contemplates under it and to provide special procedure in case the obligation under the instruments was not discharged. It has, always to be kept in mind that Section 138 of the Act creates an offence and the law relating to the penal provisions has to be interpreted strictly so Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 14 of 21 15 that no one can ingeniously or insidiously or guilefully or strategically be prosecuted". 21. Section 2(n) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 defines "offences which includes not only the doing of a Act but also omission which is punishable under any law". In C C Alavi Haji's judgment, it was categorically explained by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that if the drawer takes the plea that he should not be prosecuted for offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act by reason of not having received the notice of dishonour of cheque as mandated by Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments, then the preparation of notice and of the period of notice was still available to him on account of some practical difficulties perceived by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the process and mode of service and receiving the notice of dishonour and payment under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act as recognized by our Hon'ble Supreme Court. Hon'ble Supreme Court was of the view that sometimes indeed the notice may not actually be served upon the accused/drawer and so Hon'ble Supreme court granted this relief to a honest drawer of the cheque that even if he actually did not receive the mandatory legal notice under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, then he may treat the summons of the court issued for offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act as that mandatory notice and pay the cheque amount in question within 15 days of the receiving of summons or on coming to the court. If the drawer/accused was not liable to pay the cheque amount then situation would remain the same and accused may plead not guilty to Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 15 of 21 16 the notice framed under Section 251 CrPC and prove his defence either by bringing out material from the cross examination of complainant's witnesses or by leading his own evidence whichever suits the drawer/accused. 22. In view of the above-mentioned submissions, evidences, testimonies and material available on the record, this Court feels that the complainant has been able to prove its case beyond a reasonable shadow of doubt and that the accused has not been able to rebut the statutory presumptions either from the cross-examination of the complainant's testimony or by leading his own evidence. It is further observed that the complainant has proved his case to the satisfaction of the court and accused has not been able to prove his innocence. 23. Apex court in Rangappa vs Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 while overruling the judgment titled Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs Dattatraya G Hegde AIR 2008 SC 1325 observed in para 14 that : "the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observation in Krishna Janardhan Bhatt (supra) cannot be correct............This is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested". 24. Therefore, in view of the statutory provisions and Apex Court's Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 16 of 21 17 judgments, there is a presumption in favour of holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any legally enforceable debt or other liability. It is a well settled principle of law that the presumption available U/s 139 N I Act can be rebutted by the accused by adducing evidence. Therefore, the burden of proof is on the accused to rebutt the statutory presumption. The accused can prove the non existence of consideration by raising a probable defence and if he proves the same, then only the onus would shift upon complainant, who has to prove it as a matter of fact and his failure to prove would dis-entitle him to grant the relief. 25. Apex Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs Dattatraya G Hegde AIR 2008 Supreme Court 1325 has held as follows : "23. ...............Standard of proof on the part of an accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different". 26. Apex Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhatt 's case (supra) has also held at para 25 that : "25. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of an accused is "preponderance of probabilities". Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on records by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies". Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 17 of 21 18 27. Therefore, what has been upheld by Apex Court in the above noted case is that accused can prove his defence by "preponderance of probabilities" whereas prosecution has to prove the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts. It was also held by Apex Court in the said case that : "26. A statutory presumption has an evidentiary value. The question as to whether the presumption stood rebutted or not, must, therefore, be determined keeping in view the other evidences on record. For the said purpose, stepping into the witness box by the appellant is not imperative. In the case of this nature, where the chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration". 28. In view of the above discussion, it is clear that the defence of accused has not got proved even on the scale of preponderance of probabilities. Having considered the entire evidence, it is proved that accused had issued the cheque against liability and against legally enforceable debt and the said cheque was dishonoured due to the reason "Funds Insufficient". 29. It is proved on record that accused despite service of statutory notice of demand failed to make the payment of the cheque in question within 15 days from receipt thereof. The complainant has fulfilled all the ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Accordingly, accused Mohinder Panwar stands convicted for committing the offence U/s Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 18 of 21 19 138 Negotiable Instruments Act . Let he be heard on the point of sentence. Announced in the open court on 26/08/2013 (SUNIL BENIWAL) Metropolitan Magistrate -03/N I Act/South Saket Court/New Delhi Certified that this judgment contains 19 pages and each page bears my signature. (SUNIL BENIWAL) Metropolitan Magistrate -03/N I Act/South Saket Court/New Delhi Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 19 of 21 20 IN THE COURT OF SH SUNIL BENIWAL : METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE - 03 : SOUTH : SAKET COURT : NEW DELHI Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar CC No 123/1 U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act ORDER ON SENTENCE Present : Complainant with counsel Convict with counsel It is argued by Ld. counsel for convict that convict had been ready to pay the cheque amount right from the start of the trial. Therefore, a prayer of leniency towards convict is made by Ld. counsel. Counsel for the complainant on the contrary argues that this contention of the counsel for convict is false and convict has deliberately delayed the trial of the case and the convict never tendered the cheque amount in reality and merely offered to pay. Counsel for complainant has submitted that if the real intention of the convict was to pay the cheque amount right from the very beginning, no demand draft or cash was ever tendered by the convict till date which shows the intention of the convict that he never intended to pay. Complainant has submitted that in reality convict is liable to pay Rs.1,75,000/- to the complainant for work done but the impugned cheque is the only cheque left with the complainant because of fraud played by convict. Therefore, Ld. counsel for complainant has prayed for taking strict view under the provisions of N I Act. I have heard the submissions made by both the sides. I have also considered the circumstances of the case. Punishment awarded to the convict must be commensurate with the gravity of offence committed by the Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 20 of 21 21 convict and all the mitigating and extenuating circumstances should be looked at before awarding punishment to the convict. Therefore, keeping in view the arguments and totality of circumstances, convict is hereby sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for four months and further directed to pay a compensation of twice the cheque amount i.e. Rs.50,000/- (fifty thousand) within a period of 30 days to the complainant. In default of payment of compensation, the convict shall further undergo simple imprisonment for two months. Hence, punishment accordingly awarded. At this stage, counsel for the convict moves application for suspension of sentence under the provisions of Section 389 (3) CrPC for filing the appeal by convict and request is made for releasing him on bail. Heard. Perused. Convict is admitted on bail on his furnishing bail bond in the sum of Rs.50,000/- with one surety of the like amount. Bail bond furnished and accepted. Ordered accordingly. Announced in the open court on 30/08/2013 (SUNIL BENIWAL) Metropolitan Magistrate -03/N I Act/South Saket Court/New Delhi Afzal Ahmed vs Mohinder Panwar Page 21 of 21
